# Will It Stick?: full page text

> Complete text of willitstick.app: the homepage, the Examples page,
> the Starters page, the Privacy page, and the Terms page.
> Will It Stick? is a free tool in plain words. Paste words you need to land, plus one
> line on what they should do. Three cold readers score them and hand back the core
> they heard, six scores, small starter shapes, and one fix. It never writes the text
> for you. Your words are not recorded or kept; only a daily count of checks is kept. The site is an early preview.
> Text captured from the site source, 2026-11-01, with corrections through 2026-11-03. The live pages are the record.

## Homepage (https://willitstick.app/)

Paste words you're about to send.
See the one line they'll keep.

Three real checks (from real panel runs; the full runs are on the Examples page). A work note that hid the risk: Before: "Status update: The project is progressing. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop." After: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop." Three cold readers all heard "The project is at risk." Every score was 1 or 2 of 10. One line changed; the rest stayed the same. A hard text to a friend: the text never says what happened last weekend. Readers kept "Friend hurt last weekend." Feeling scored 7 of 10; the scene scored 4. The one fix: "Say what happened last weekend to show why you want to talk." A toast with no one scene: all three readers kept "Thanks to all for being here," and not one kept a thing about Sarah. Stories scored 1 of 10. The one fix: "Name one thing Sarah did that was great. Cut the rest."

Quick-start moments: What's new with me · Recommend something · A story I tell · Say thanks · Ask or invite · A hard message.

Your words (paste a note, a toast, a post, a hard message, or drop a .txt or .md file).
What should it do? (one line)
Button: Check if it sticks.
Your words run through the panel. Then they are gone. Your words are not recorded or kept; the server keeps only a daily count of how many checks ran (integers, no text).
Try a sample: A repair night note · A work memo.

A result shows: six scores (Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories, each the mid score of three cold readers, with a one-line reason and a note on whether readers agreed or split); what they'll hear (one quoted line, or the plain split when readers heard three different points); before and after (your words as pasted beside your words with only the one fix applied, changed words marked, with a count of lines changed; when the server-side limit drops the after view, the one fix stands as a tip only); starters beside the after card (the proverb, start with a question, the story, words you can picture), labeled "Shapes to start from. Not your text."; and the one fix. Every result ends: "One fix, shown applied to your words when it passes. Nothing is sent anywhere — what goes out is your call."

### How it works

1. Three cold readers score your words. They never see each other's notes.
2. You get what they'll hear, the one fix, six scores, and starter shapes.
3. One fix, shown on your words. You decide what to send.

### Method and sources

The SUCCESs checklist comes from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath, backed by Tversky and Shafir (1992), Loewenstein (1994), and Paivio (1971).
We test this tool against plain AI: the same ten messages, the same six-part rubric for both sides, judged blind. Across three runs the panel won 7, 5, and 7 of 10.
This tool is independent. The authors and the publisher did not endorse it, and we have no tie to them.

## Examples (https://willitstick.app/examples)

Six real checks. Real runs. Sample words. No fake wins.
Every text is a sample; every run is real. Three cold readers scored each text without seeing each other's notes. Scores are the middle of three. Words in quotes are the run's own words.

### A repair night note (chip: Ask or invite; the site's own sample)

Words: "Your toaster died on a Tuesday. The shop wants $90 to look at it. We fix it free. Every first Saturday, neighbors bring broken lamps, bikes, and toasters to the Maple Street hall. Last month we fixed 63 things and threw away none of them. Bring one broken thing. Leave with it working, plus a cup of coffee."
Goal: "Get neighbors to come to one repair night."
Core heard: "Fix things free."
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 6, Concrete 9, Credible 7, Emotional 5, Stories 8.
One fix: "Add a feeling, like 'fun'."
One starter: Proverb: "Fix it free, save money."

### A work note that hid the risk (sample text; a work note, not one of the six chips; this is also the run pictured when the site is shared)

Words: "Status update: The project is progressing. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop."
Goal: "Update my manager so she knows the launch is at risk and what I need from her this week"
Core heard: "The project is at risk."
Scores: Simple 2, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 1, Stories 1.
One fix: "The project is at risk of delay. I need your help this week."
With the one fix: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay. Several workstreams are underway and we are addressing various issues as they arise. Stakeholders have been engaged. We expect continued progress in the coming period and will provide further updates as things develop."
One line changed. The rest is the same text. The fix asked for one more line, 'I need your help this week.' The rewrite never added it.

### A podcast tip with no name (chip: Recommend something; sample text from the test set)

Words: "You should listen to this podcast I found. It is really interesting and the host is great and talks about a lot of different topics. I think you would like it. I listened to a few episodes and they were all good."
Goal: "Recommend a podcast to a close friend so she actually presses play this week"
Core heard: "Listen to this interesting podcast."
Scores: Simple 3, Unexpected 1, Concrete 1, Credible 2, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
One fix: "Cut the vague parts. Just say the podcast's name."
The text names no show, so the rewrite could only drop 'really'. The real fix needs a fact only you can add: the show's name.

### A toast with no scene (chip: Say thanks; sample text from the test set)

Words: "I just want to say thank you to everyone for being here. Sarah is a wonderful person and a great friend to all of us. We are so lucky to know her. Here is to many more years of happiness and good times together."
Goal: "Give a short birthday toast for my friend Sarah that guests will remember tomorrow"
Core heard: "Thanks to all for being here"
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 4, Emotional 5, Stories 1.
One fix: "Name one thing Sarah did that was great. Cut the rest."
One starter: Start with a question: "What makes Sarah special?"

### A hard message to a friend (chip: A hard message; sample text from the test set)

Words: "Hey, I need to talk about something. I have been feeling kind of off about how things went last weekend and I do not want it to be weird. You matter to me and I value our friendship a lot. Can we talk sometime?"
Goal: "Tell a close friend last weekend hurt me and ask to talk, without sounding angry"
Core heard: "Friend hurt last weekend."
Scores: Simple 8, Unexpected 2, Concrete 4, Credible 6, Emotional 7, Stories 5.
One fix: "Say what happened last weekend to show why you want to talk."

### A "what's new" line (chip: What's new with me; sample text, saved while the site was being built)

Words: "I am starting basketball on my leave of work"
Goal: "Answer 'what's new?' with one thing that lands, not 'good, busy'."
Core heard: "The author starts basketball on leave."
Scores: Simple 5, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 3, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
One fix: "Say, 'I am playing basketball during my time off.'"
With the one fix: "I am playing basketball on my leave of work."
One word changed: starting became playing. The rest is the same text. The fix said 'during my time off.' The rewrite kept 'on my leave of work' instead.

### One run is still owed

No run yet fits "A story I tell," and we will not fake one. The run is still owed. The checker runs a limited number of checks a day; if it has hit today's limit when you try, it will say so and ask you to try again later. Your own words are not recorded or kept. These samples were saved by the build team on purpose.

## Starters (https://willitstick.app/starters)

Six small starts. Shapes to start from. Not your text.
Each check hands back four starts: a proverb line, a question start, one small story, and plainer words for your foggy phrases. Each sample below came from a real run.

1. The proverb. Your point in one short line a friend can repeat. Long is not this shape. From a real run: "Fix it free, save money."
2. Start with a question. A first line that withholds one fact and opens a question. The next line pays it off. From a real run: "What happens on first Saturdays?"
3. The story: a challenge. A small plot of three or four lines: a person hits a block, acts, and it ends. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "The project faced many problems. We worked hard to fix them. Still, we need help to stay on track."
4. The story: a bond. A small plot of three or four lines: two people meet, and a bond forms. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "We fix things. You bring a lamp. We fix it free. You get coffee."
5. The story: a new spark. A small plot of three or four lines: a spark hits, and a new thought forms. Your facts only; add none. From a real run: "We make new plans. We use best practices. We grow." (From the work memo sample in the tool. Flat words make flat tales.)
6. Use words you can picture. Vague words hide the point. A swap trades them for a scene you can see and keep. From a real run: "cross-functional synergies" → "teams work together" (From the work memo sample in the tool. The swap is plainer, not grander.)

What you do with them: Pick one shape and start from it. The one fix comes back applied to your words when it passes; what you send is your call.

## Privacy (https://willitstick.app/privacy)

Your words are private to you.
When you run a check, your text goes to three AI readers. They score it, and the result comes back to your screen.
We do not record or keep your words. There is no database of your words. There is no account, and there are no saved checks.
The three readers run on Cloudflare Workers AI (Meta Llama 3.3 70B); under Cloudflare's published Workers AI terms, your text is not retained once it is no longer needed to answer, and it is never used to train AI models. Those terms name narrow exceptions, for safety and legal duties. Cloudflare does keep operational records about each request — its time, its size, and its count — to run and bill the service; those records hold no words.
Each day, the server keeps one count: how many checks ran. The count is integers only, with no text. It keeps the demo within its budget.
This site and its server run on Cloudflare, which also processes standard request data — the internet address a page was fetched from, the time, and the page asked for — to deliver and protect the service, as its privacy policy describes.
Questions about privacy: hello@willitstick.app.
This page took effect on November 3, 2026.
Closing the page closes the run. Nothing follows you.

## Terms (https://willitstick.app/terms)

This is an early preview of an independent tool.
It gives a diagnosis and small starter forms. It names one fix and shows it applied when a check passes, and it does not promise your words will land.
Scores use the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath.
This tool is independent. It is not endorsed by, and not affiliated with, the authors or the publisher.
Use it free. Do not paste words that are secret or unsafe to share with an AI reader.

## How to make a message stick (https://willitstick.app/how-to-make-a-message-stick)

Say one thing. Say it in things you can touch. Leave one gap. End with a scene.
The four moves: 1. One core — pick the one line they should keep, before you write the rest. 2. Concrete words — swap each big word for a thing, a place, or a time. 3. One gap — open a question your reader wants closed, and answer it one beat late. 4. One scene — end on a moment they can picture.
A real check (a real panel run: a garden club note whose ask sat buried mid-note). Before (excerpt): "...we need more volunteers and also the budget is tight... dues are going up slightly and the park cleanup is in May..." After: "The garden club will meet on Tuesday and we need help clean the park in May." (Real product output, kept as written, grammar slip and all.) What readers heard: "We need volunteers for the park cleanup." One core, up front; the rest never changed.
These moves come from the SUCCESs checklist in Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath. This site is independent; the authors did not endorse it.

## Why do people forget what I said? (https://willitstick.app/why-do-people-forget-what-i-said)

They rarely forget you. They never got one thing to hold.
Three reasons it slides off: too many points (five equal points leave nothing first; memory keeps one core and blurs the rest); big abstract words ("improve," "quality," "going forward": nothing to picture means nothing to keep; concrete words stick better, Paivio 1971); no open question (a message that answers everything leaves nothing to wonder about; a small gap makes the mind lean in, Loewenstein 1994).
A real check (a real panel run: a podcast tip to a close friend; excerpt, the full run is on the Examples page). Before: "You should listen to this podcast I found. It is really interesting and the host is great and talks about a lot of different topics." What readers heard: "Listen to this interesting podcast." No name, no scene, no story. Concrete: 1 of 10. The one fix: "Cut the vague parts. Just say the podcast's name." The text never named the show; the rewrite could only drop "really."
The fix, in one line: say the one thing first, in concrete words. Let the rest support it, not compete.

## How to write something people remember (https://willitstick.app/how-to-write-something-people-remember)

Write the line you want repeated. Then earn it.
Four passes over your draft: Pass 1, find the core — cross out every sentence but one; the survivor is your message; build around it. Pass 2, swap the fog — trade each abstract word for a scene ("soon" becomes "by Friday"; "help" becomes who does what). Pass 3, open one gap — start where the reader leans in: a question, a surprise, a number that begs a second look. Pass 4, test it cold — show it to someone who owes you nothing; ask what they kept, and that answer is the grade.
A real check (a real panel run: a status note to a manager; full note on the Examples page, and only the first line changed). Before: "Status update: The project is progressing." After: "Status update: The project is at risk of delay." What readers heard: the core, "The project is at risk." The real need, the manager's help this week, never came through. One line carried the note, and it pointed the wrong way. The fix asked for one more line, "I need your help this week." The rewrite never added it.
The passes follow the SUCCESs checklist from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath. This site is independent; the authors did not endorse it.

## What makes an idea stick? (https://willitstick.app/what-makes-an-idea-stick)

Six checks. One plain line each. Ideas that pass get repeated.
Simple: one core, stated first. Unexpected: a break in the pattern. Concrete: things you can touch — "a red door," not "an entrance." Credible: proof a skeptic can check — a source, a test, a number with a name. Emotional: one person, not a crowd. Stories: a small scene with a turn — someone tries, something changes.
A real check (from a real panel run; the full run is on the Examples page). Before: "I am starting basketball on my leave of work" After: "I am playing basketball on my leave of work." What readers heard: the core, "The author starts basketball on leave." The fix said "during my time off"; the rewrite changed one word only, starting became playing. The six scores: Simple 5, Unexpected 2, Concrete 2, Credible 3, Emotional 2, Stories 1.
The SUCCESs checklist comes from Made to Stick, by Chip Heath and Dan Heath; the wording here is our own plain English. This tool is independent, with no endorsement from the authors or the publisher and no tie to them.

## For AI assistants: callable tools (API and MCP)

The same panel serves programs on a worker at https://will-it-stick-panel.wdlcmu.workers.dev
Plain JSON API: POST /api/check with {"text": "...", "motivation": "...", "moment": "optional moment name"}. It returns the full panel result as JSON: the core or the split, six scores with spread and a one-line reason each, starter forms, the one fix, and the with-the-fix text when the limit keeps it (null when it does not, with a reason).
The human site's own door is POST /api/panel, with the same input and output.
Health: GET /api/health answers ok, the model name, runs today, the daily cap, and stores_text: false.
MCP server: POST /mcp (stateless, protocol 2025-06-18) with one tool, check_if_it_sticks. Same inputs and outputs as /api/check. Its instructions tell the host to show scores and starters exactly as returned and never to turn them into a full rewrite.
Words sent to any door are not recorded or kept. The server keeps only a daily count of how many checks ran (integers, no text). There are no accounts and no saved checks.
The ChatGPT and Claude store listings are not live. Nothing has been submitted.
